source.title: Convergence and Divergence of Language Models under Different Random Seeds
source.authors: F. Fehlauer; Kyle Mahowald; Tiago Pimentel

record.file_problem: None; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures predictive-distribution convergence across training seeds and model sizes. It finds non-monotonic convergence, slower or absent reconvergence in smaller models, and variation by token/context, refining the scope of convergence claims. Its outcome is predictive-distribution similarity, not representation geometry.
record.gate_note: The study operationalizes convergence as negative expected per-token KL divergence between models trained with different seeds. Results therefore bear on the claim's convergence and context-dependence aspects using an output-distribution measure, but do not directly measure representational distances, shared features, or shared subspaces. Figure values are not available in the supplied text, so rows report only the authors' explicit textual descriptions.
record.test_reason: The study measures how similar the next-token output distributions of same-architecture models trained from different seeds are, using per-token KL. It measures no internal representations, features, subspaces, mappings or cross-family alignment. The construct is related to the claim (output convergence across seeds and sizes) but differs from every version, which all concern representations. The PRH is cited only in a footnote as a stronger claim. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that seed-to-seed predictive convergence goes through four phases while cross-entropy falls monotonically. They add that larger models reconverge faster while the smallest never really reconverge, suggesting a minimum size is needed for stable distributions. Frequent tokens and function words converge faster and more reliably than rare tokens and content words.
record.recipe_differences: Uses expected negative per-token KL divergence between next-token distributions, rather than measuring representational distances between inputs. The study focuses on seed replicas and training dynamics. The paper lists the repository path Tr1ple-F/convergence-and-divergence-of-llms.
record.method_sensitivity: Convergence varies with training phase and model size, and with token frequency, part of speech, final surprisal, and context. BLiMP and MultiBERT show related but not identical coverage; early MultiBERT checkpoints are unavailable.

fits_no_version.finding: Output-distribution convergence across seeds (negative expected per-token KL) is non-monotonic over training in four phases: uniform, sharp convergence, sharp divergence, then slow reconvergence. This happens while cross-entropy falls monotonically. The later phases are also seen on BLiMP and in MultiBERT.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Seed replicas of a language model converge and diverge in their predictive distributions in distinct training phases. They can become less similar to each other while all fitting the data better.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger Pythia models (up to 410m) reconverge faster late in training. The smallest models end with similar E[conv] to their initial value. In the Appendix D regression, the model-size coefficients later show larger models raising conv and smaller models lowering it (Fig. 8 right; not a row).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Seed-to-seed agreement of output distributions increases with model size late in training. Small models may never reconverge.

fits_no_version.finding: Output convergence depends on the token. Frequent tokens and function words converge more; rare tokens and content words diverge, with final convergence below initial. Very-low-surprisal tokens converge strongly. Variance across contexts rises in the later phases. Appendix C: for the 410m model, noun subtypes end at or below their starting convergence (not a row).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Agreement between seed replicas' predictions is uneven across inputs, concentrated on frequent and predictable tokens.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 2025
record.problems: The analysis uses a small subset of the Pile validation set covering 4,662 tokens and English-only data. Computational constraints limit the seed sample to seeds 1, 3, 5, 7, and 9. The token-level KL measure prevents comparison across model families with different tokenizers. Early MultiBERT checkpoints are missing. Learning-rate warm-up may introduce artifacts. Many numerical results are shown only in figures, and direct representation similarity is not measured.
record.rows_left_out: No separately quantified values could be extracted from figure-only plots because the supplied text does not include the plotted coordinates. Appendix C's noun and verb subtype results and Appendix F's example-token KL listings are not included as rows because they are token-level subdivisions or examples rather than separately reported model-level convergence findings relevant to these versions.

untested.parts: No representational alignment is measured. Only output KL among seed replicas of one architecture is reported; different architectures, objectives and data are not compared.
Seeds are compared, but only on output distributions. No features, units or subspaces are compared.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation experiments.
No interpretable features or circuits are compared across models.
No representational similarity metric or its settings is varied. Only a single output KL measure is used.
Representational alignment and its causes (shared data or objectives) are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V1, V6 and V7, but the study measures output-distribution KL across same-architecture seeds, not representations. Under the gate rules this is a related but different construct, so no version verdicts are given. It is arguably closest to V3 (seeds) and to V1's scale trend, but it measures no features, subspaces or cross-family representations. The paper's citation of Huh et al. is a footnote only. Numeric figure values are not in the text.

versions.untested_parts: Tests scale-related convergence among seed replicas in the Pythia suite using predictive-distribution KL, not representation-distance geometry. Different architectures, objectives, training data, modalities, and alignment across independently developed model families are not tested; the study does not establish that larger models are more capable in a broad sense.
No vision-language models or paired image-caption representations are analyzed.
Different seeds of the same architecture are compared, but the study does not measure features, units, or shared representation subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired interchangeability experiment is conducted.
No interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are identified across models.
The study varies token/context properties and evaluates an additional task and model family, but does not compare similarity metrics or their settings, and does not test out-of-distribution inputs.
The study reports incomplete, non-monotonic, and size-dependent convergence, but does not test whether shared training data or objectives cause alignment rather than a common model of reality.

rows.subject: Pythia model suite (models of 14m, 31m, 70m, 160m, and 410m parameters; seed-level results summarized across sizes)
rows.operation_detail: Estimated expected negative per-token KL divergence across independently seeded models.

conditions.value: four phases: roughly through step 16; steps 16–256; steps 256–2k; from around step 2k

rows.measure: Expected convergence E[conv], defined as negative expected KL divergence between seed-trained models' next-token distributions.
rows.baseline: Initial training convergence; numeric value not stated.
rows.value: Text describes an initial near-uniform phase, sharp convergence, sharp divergence, then slow reconvergence; the plotted values are not stated in the text.
rows.uncertainty: 1σ confidence intervals shown in Figure 1; numeric intervals not stated.
rows.note: The authors explicitly describe the four phases. The outcome is predictive-distribution similarity, not a direct measure of representation geometry.
rows.check: Measures seed-to-seed output-distribution KL in Pythia, not representational alignment. It does not bear on V1 (different architectures, data and objectives) or on V7's representational alignment.

rows.subject: Smallest Pythia models (individual sizes not stated for this finding)
rows.operation_detail: Compared expected convergence at the end of training with its initial value across seeds.
rows.measure: Expected negative KL divergence across seeds.
rows.baseline: Initial E[conv]; numeric value not stated.
rows.value: The smallest models mostly stabilize and end with similar E[conv] to their initial values; the authors say they do not converge to a shared solution.
rows.uncertainty: 1σ confidence intervals shown in Figure 1; numeric intervals not stated.
rows.note: The paper does not assign this textual result to a particular listed size, so the subject remains the smallest models as described.
rows.check: Output-distribution measure. The 'smallest models' are not identified by size. The finding concerns seed replicas, not independently designed models.

rows.subject: Larger Pythia models (individual sizes not stated for this finding)
rows.operation_detail: Compared the steepness of late-training reconvergence across model sizes.
rows.measure: Rate of increase in expected convergence E[conv].
rows.baseline: Smaller model sizes; numeric value not stated.
rows.value: Larger models reconverge faster than smaller models; numeric values are not stated.
rows.uncertainty: 1σ confidence intervals shown in Figure 1; numeric intervals not stated.
rows.note: The result concerns seed-to-seed predictive distributions and late-training reconvergence, rather than representational distances.
rows.check: Faster late reconvergence for larger models is about output KL across seeds, not representation alignment across model families.

rows.subject: Pythia model suite evaluated on BLiMP
rows.operation_detail: Computed seed-to-seed KL convergence on the BLiMP grammatical-versus-ungrammatical sentence distributions.
rows.measure: Expected convergence on the restricted two-sentence BLiMP distributions.
rows.value: The downstream convergence pattern broadly mirrors the phases observed on the Pile validation subset; numeric values are not stated.
rows.uncertainty: 1σ̄ confidence intervals shown in Figure 2; numeric intervals not stated.
rows.note: The paper reports this as a task-level result for the same predictive-distribution convergence measure.
rows.check: Output-distribution convergence restricted to BLiMP sentence pairs. No representation measure.

rows.subject: MultiBERT model suite
rows.stage_stated: available checkpoints; checkpoints between 0 and 20k are unavailable
rows.operation_detail: Computed seed-to-seed KL convergence for masked language models.

conditions.value: available checkpoints only; early checkpoints unavailable

rows.value: The observed later dynamics include sharp divergence followed by slow reconvergence; the initial uniform and sharp-convergence phases could not be observed.
rows.uncertainty: 1σ confidence intervals shown in Figure 2; numeric intervals not stated.
rows.note: Only the remaining later dynamics could be compared because early MultiBERT checkpoints were unavailable.
rows.check: MultiBERT output (masked-LM) distribution convergence across seeds. No representation measure.

rows.subject: Selected Pythia models (individual sizes not stated in the text)
rows.stage_stated: training phases three and four; final checkpoint comparison
rows.operation_detail: Estimated conditional seed-to-seed convergence for tokens grouped by frequency.
rows.measure: Conditional expected convergence by token frequency.
rows.baseline: Initial convergence for the reported comparison; numeric value not stated.
rows.value: Frequent-token convergence stabilizes at a relatively high value; infrequent tokens undergo sharp divergence, and their final convergence is below their initial convergence.
rows.uncertainty: 1σ confidence intervals shown in Figure 3; numeric intervals not stated.
rows.note: The authors describe clear dependence on which tokens are evaluated; the plotted category values are not available in the supplied text.
rows.check: Conditional output convergence by token frequency. This is input dependence of an output-KL measure, not of a representational similarity metric (V6).

rows.subject: Selected Pythia models (individual sizes not stated in the text)
rows.operation_detail: Estimated conditional seed-to-seed convergence for tokens grouped by part of speech.
rows.measure: Conditional expected convergence by part of speech.
rows.value: Content words (nouns, adjectives, and verbs) diverge more in the sharp-divergence phase; function words have higher final convergence, while content words remain more divergent.
rows.uncertainty: 1σ confidence intervals shown in Figure 3; numeric intervals not stated.
rows.note: The authors note that frequency and part of speech may be correlated.
rows.check: Conditional output convergence by part of speech. Not a representational similarity measure.

rows.subject: Selected Pythia models (individual sizes not stated in the text)
rows.operation_detail: Estimated conditional seed-to-seed convergence for tokens grouped by final surprisal.
rows.measure: Conditional expected convergence by final surprisal.
rows.value: Very-low-final-surprisal tokens show strong convergence by the end; tokens with final surprisal from 1 to 8+ bits have broadly similar convergence behavior.
rows.uncertainty: 1σ confidence intervals shown in Figure 3; numeric intervals not stated.
rows.note: Convergence differs by predictability for very predictable tokens, while the reported higher-surprisal bins are similar to one another.
rows.check: Conditional output convergence by final surprisal. Not a representational similarity measure.

rows.subject: Pythia models across analyzed sizes
rows.operation_detail: Measured variance of per-context convergence across contexts.

conditions.value: contexts in the Pile validation subset
initial two versus final two convergence phases

rows.baseline: Initial two training phases; numeric variance not stated.
rows.value: The initial two phases have very little variance across contexts; the final two phases show a significant increase in variance.
rows.uncertainty: Shaded areas in Figure 4 represent standard deviation across contexts; numeric values not stated.
rows.note: This reports context dependence of the measured convergence; it does not compare alternative similarity metrics.
rows.check: Variance of output convergence across contexts. Not a representational similarity measure.

rows.subject: Pythia models across analyzed sizes
rows.operation_detail: Regressed per-context convergence on token frequency, part of speech, and model size.

conditions.value: one linear regression per training step

rows.measure: Regression coefficient for log token frequency predicting conv(s<t).
rows.baseline: Coefficient initially close to zero; numeric value not stated.
rows.value: Around step 256, frequency begins to positively influence conv, with α ≈ 0.05; the correlation increases slightly thereafter.
rows.note: The authors interpret this as frequent tokens stabilizing earlier and showing lower KL divergence across seeds.
rows.check: Regression of output convergence on log frequency (α≈0.05 around step 256). Value is correct but bears on no version.
